case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a civil RICO plaintiff suffers an injury to “business or property” when the only alleged RICO damages are economic losses (such as lost earnings) that flow from a personal injury.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1964(c) (civil RICO), specifically the requirement that a private plaintiff be “injured in his business or property by reason of” a RICO violation.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that § 1964(c) does not allow recovery for losses that are derivative of personal injuries (e.g., lost wages/earning capacity, medical expenses) because those are not injuries to “business or property” within the meaning of civil RICO; allowing such claims would transform RICO into a treble-damages personal-injury/tort regime and massively expand liability beyond what Congress authorized.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues that although personal injuries themselves are not compensable under civil RICO, the economic consequences of those injuries—particularly “loss of earnings” damages—are injuries to “business or property” and therefore are recoverable if proximately caused “by reason of” the defendant’s racketeering conduct; respondent also resists imposing extra-textual limits on RICO standing beyond what the statute requires.
key_precedents: Sedima, S.P.R.L. v. Imrex Co., 473 U.S. 479 (1985)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest contention—that lost wages and medical expenses are quintessential economic harms and therefore injuries to “property”—still cannot be reconciled with the restrictive significance this Court has consistently given the Clayton Act–derived phrase “business or property.” Justice Thomas’s point is decisive for me: if we treat the economic sequelae of bodily injury as “property,” the statutory line collapses and § 1964(c) effectively becomes a treble-damages personal-injury regime, a major shift Congress did not clearly enact. Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh properly read Sedima as rejecting atextual barriers, not as authorizing us to disregard textual limits; enforcing “business or property” is the narrowest, most administrable ground and avoids broader pronouncements about RICO’s scope or proximate cause. No colleague has identified precedent undermining Reiter’s reading of the identical Clayton Act language; if anything, Holmes (as Justice Thomas notes) reinforces that § 1964(c) incorporates traditional boundaries on cognizable injury and prevents derivative tort recoveries from ballooning into federal RICO litigation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument—that medical bills and lost wages are economic harms and therefore “property”—fails because § 1964(c) does not cover all economic loss; it limits suits to injury to “business or property,” a phrase of art borrowed from the Clayton Act and given “restrictive significance” in Reiter to exclude personal injuries and their repackaged components. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, accepting respondent’s framing would collapse Congress’s textual line and effectively convert civil RICO into a treble-damages personal-injury regime, which the statute’s words do not authorize. Justice Kavanaugh’s reference to RJR Nabisco reinforces that “business or property” is a real, continuing constraint, and Holmes further counsels against expanding RICO to derivative tort-like harms that would invite remote and sprawling litigation. No colleague identified any precedent that undercuts the original public meaning of “business or property” as excluding personal-injury damages and their economic incidents.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that lost wages and medical bills are economic harms and therefore injuries to “property”—has surface appeal, but it cannot be reconciled with the restrictive significance this Court has given the identical Clayton Act phrase. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, reading “business or property” to include any pecuniary consequence of bodily injury collapses Congress’s textual line and effectively converts § 1964(c) into a treble-damages personal-injury regime, a major expansion not supported by the statutory words. Justice Kavanaugh’s reminder about RJR Nabisco reinforces that we have continued to treat § 1964(c)’s standing language as a real constraint, while Holmes (as Thomas notes) underscores the administrability and remoteness problems that would predictably follow from recognizing derivative personal-injury losses. Sedima’s caution against atextual barriers does not help respondent because enforcing the “business or property” limit is textual fidelity, not judicial embellishment.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains that medical bills and lost wages are concrete pecuniary harms that intuitively resemble “property” loss, and Sedima cautions against judge-made narrowing of civil RICO. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief stress, honoring § 1964(c)’s “business or property” limit is not an extra-textual hurdle; Reiter’s reading of the identical Clayton Act language as having “restrictive significance” makes it difficult to treat the economic components of a personal-injury claim as independently cognizable without erasing Congress’s line. Justice Thomas’s administrability/text concern is persuasive for me: if every downstream economic consequence of bodily harm counts, the person/property distinction collapses and civil RICO functionally becomes a treble-damages personal-injury regime—a major shift better left to Congress. Pragmatically, that expansion would likely advantage sophisticated repeat litigants and create sprawling federal litigation, while leaving vulnerable plaintiffs no better off than traditional state tort pathways.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that lost wages and medical bills are economic harms to “property,” and Sedima cautions against judge-made narrowing—doesn’t overcome the statute’s own limiting words: “business or property” is not a synonym for “any economic consequence.” As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Reiter’s reading of the identical Clayton Act phrase as having “restrictive significance” excluding personal injuries makes it difficult to treat the economic components of a personal-injury claim as independently cognizable under § 1964(c) without draining that limitation of content. Justice Thomas’s administrability concern also matters under my pragmatic textualism: if downstream pecuniary effects suffice, civil RICO becomes a treble-damages personal-injury regime, and courts will be forced into an unstable line-drawing exercise between “derivative” and “independent” losses. RJR Nabisco and Holmes, cited by Justice Thomas and others, reinforce that § 1964(c) is a real constraint and that we should not read it in a way that expands liability in precisely the sprawling fashion those cases warn against.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that lost wages and medical expenses are quintessentially economic and might be labeled “property,” but that argument reads § 1964(c) as if it said “any economic loss” rather than “business or property.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, this Court has given the Clayton Act’s identical phrase “restrictive significance,” and under Reiter and Truett Payne the relevant question is whether the claimed dollars are simply a measure of personal injury; allowing those derivative components would erase the statutory line and effectively create a treble-damages personal-injury regime. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on RJR Nabisco reinforces that we continue to treat “business or property” as a real textual constraint, while Holmes underscores the traditional limits on actionable injury that counsel against opening RICO to derivative tort-like losses. Sedima warns against judge-made barriers, but enforcing Congress’s own words is the opposite of that; any expansion to cover personal-injury sequelae must come from Congress, not us.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest argument remains that lost wages and medical bills are paradigmatic economic harms and thus “property,” and Sedima cautions against judge-made narrowing of civil RICO. But as Chief Justice Roberts persuasively explains, “injured in his business or property” is a term of art borrowed from Clayton Act § 4 that this Court (Reiter) has treated as carrying restrictive significance excluding personal-injury harms, and re-labeling the economic sequelae of bodily injury would effectively nullify that line. Justice Thomas’s point, reinforced by RJR Nabisco, that we have continued to treat § 1964(c)’s standing language as a genuine limitation—and not a mere label—supports a historically grounded, administrable boundary that avoids converting civil RICO into a treble-damages personal-injury regime. Sedima is not undermined by this approach because we are not adding an atextual barrier; we are enforcing the statute’s express words as understood in their settled lineage.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—that lost wages and medical bills are economic and therefore “property”—still fails because it treats “business or property” as synonymous with “any pecuniary loss,” contrary to the phrase’s ordinary public meaning and its settled, restrictive construction in the Clayton Act line. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Reiter is persuasive: if personal injuries are excluded, plaintiffs cannot evade that boundary by redescribing quintessential elements of a personal-injury recovery as property loss. Justice Thomas’s administrability and statutory-structure point reinforces the textual analysis: accepting derivative economic consequences of bodily harm would effectively convert § 1964(c) into a treble-damages personal-injury regime, a major expansion not fairly grounded in the words Congress chose. Colleagues’ references to Holmes and RJR Nabisco do not undermine this view; they instead confirm that § 1964(c) contains meaningful limiting principles that we must enforce rather than dilute.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument—that medical bills and lost wages are concrete economic harms and therefore “property” injuries—fails because it would let litigants re-label the economic incidents of bodily harm to evade Congress’s “business or property” limitation. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Reiter’s characterization of the identical Clayton Act phrase as having “restrictive significance” is especially persuasive to me because it provides a text-and-precedent anchor for keeping personal-injury damages (and their derivative components) outside § 1964(c). Justice Thomas’s invocation of RJR Nabisco and Holmes strengthens the administrability and boundary-setting concerns: treating downstream pecuniary effects of physical injury as “property” would effectively treble-damage vast swaths of ordinary tort law and invite remote, sprawling litigation. Under a pragmatic fairness lens, enforcing this clear standing line respects Congress’s remedial choice and preserves workable, predictable access to federal courts without converting RICO into a general personal-injury supplement.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1964(c) authorizes suit only by a person “injured in his business or property,” and that phrase—borrowed from § 4 of the Clayton Act—has “restrictive significance” that excludes personal injuries and, by the same logic, economic losses that are derivative of those personal injuries. Reiter v. Sonotone Corp., 442 U.S. 330, 339 (1979), makes clear that “business or property” does not encompass “damages for personal injuries,” and this Court has similarly contrasted recoverable “business damages” with “damages resulting from a personal injury.” J. Truett Payne Co. v. Chrysler Motors Corp., 451 U.S. 557, 566 (1981). Reading § 1964(c) to reach lost earnings and medical expenses flowing from bodily injury would effectively convert civil RICO into a treble-damages personal-injury regime, an expansion better left to Congress and inconsistent with a narrow, text- and precedent-grounded construction. Sedima rejected extra-textual standing barriers, but it did not authorize rewriting the statute’s “business or property” limitation, which here provides the narrow basis to decide the case.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1964(c) authorizes suit only by one “injured in his business or property,” and that text—tracking the Clayton Act—uses restrictive terms that exclude personal injuries and the derivative components of a personal-injury recovery (medical expenses and lost wages). See 18 U.S.C. § 1964(c); Reiter v. Sonotone Corp., 442 U.S. 330, 338 (1979) ("business or property" is restrictive); RJR Nabisco, Inc. v. European Cmty., 579 U.S. 325, 350 (2016) (same). Allowing treble-damages RICO claims whenever a personal injury produces economic loss would collapse the statute’s person/property distinction and transform RICO into a general tort enhancer—an expansion the text does not permit. Holmes v. Securities Investor Protection Corp., 503 U.S. 258 (1992), reinforces that § 1964(c)’s limits reflect common-law understandings of causation and injury and do not extend to remote, derivative harms.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1964(c) authorizes suit only for those “injured in [their] business or property,” and that limiting phrase has “restrictive significance” that excludes personal injuries and, with them, damages that are merely derivative of personal injury such as lost earnings and medical expenses. Reiter v. Sonotone Corp., 442 U.S. 330, 339 (1979), interpreting identical Clayton Act language, confirms that “business or property” excludes personal-injury-type harms, and this Court has routinely construed civil RICO’s standing language in parallel with antitrust. Allowing treble-damages recovery whenever a personal injury produces economic consequences would effectively convert civil RICO into a generalized personal-injury regime, a sweeping expansion with serious practical consequences for liability and law-enforcement-adjacent actors that Congress did not clearly authorize in the statutory text. Sedima, S.P.R.L. v. Imrex Co., 473 U.S. 479 (1985), warns against importing extra-textual standing barriers, but it does not permit courts to erase the statute’s textual limitation to injuries to “business or property.”

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1964(c) limits civil RICO standing to those “injured in [their] business or property,” and this Court has treated that identical phrase in the Clayton Act as having “restrictive significance” that “exclude[s] personal injuries.” Reiter v. Sonotone Corp., 442 U.S. 330, 339 (1979); see also J. Truett Payne Co. v. Chrysler Motors Corp., 451 U.S. 557, 566 (1981) (distinguishing business damages from “damages resulting from a personal injury”). Where the only alleged RICO damages are lost earnings or medical costs that merely flow from a personal injury, the injury remains personal in character and thus falls outside § 1964(c)’s text. While I am attentive to real-world harms, expanding RICO to treble-damages personal-injury derivatives would be a major shift better left to Congress, and traditional tort remedies remain available.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1964(c) authorizes suit only for a plaintiff “injured in his business or property,” and that phrase has long been read as carrying “restrictive significance” that excludes personal injuries and attempts to recast them as economic loss. Given RICO’s adoption of the Clayton Act’s identical “business or property” language, Reiter v. Sonotone Corp. supports treating lost earnings and medical expenses that merely flow from a personal injury as outside the statute’s remedial scope. This reading also preserves statutory coherence and workability by preventing civil RICO from becoming a treble-damages personal-injury regime untethered from Congress’s textual limitation. Sedima cautions against importing atextual standing hurdles, but enforcing the “business or property” boundary is textual, not an extra-statutory barrier.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1964(c) authorizes suit only for one “injured in his business or property,” and the ordinary meaning of that limiting phrase excludes personal injuries and damages derivative of them. This Court has read identical language in the Clayton Act as carrying “restrictive significance” that “exclude[s] personal injuries,” Reiter v. Sonotone Corp., 442 U.S. 330, 339 (1979), and has distinguished recoverable “business damages” from “damages resulting from a personal injury,” J. Truett Payne Co. v. Chrysler Motors Corp., 451 U.S. 557, 566 (1981). Sedima instructs courts not to add extra-textual standing hurdles, but it does not permit courts to erase textual limits Congress chose; treating lost wages and medical expenses as “business or property” would effectively convert civil RICO into a treble-damages personal-injury regime beyond § 1964(c)’s terms.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1964(c) authorizes suit only for a person “injured in his business or property,” and that limiting phrase—borrowed verbatim from § 4 of the Clayton Act—has long been understood to exclude personal-injury harms and derivative economic losses. In Reiter v. Sonotone Corp., 442 U.S. 330, 339 (1979), the Court described “business or property” as having “restrictive significance” that “exclude[s] personal injuries,” and antitrust cases have treated damages “resulting from a personal injury” as outside that text. Sedima, S.P.R.L. v. Imrex Co., 473 U.S. 479 (1985), warns against importing extra-textual standing barriers, but it does not permit courts to erase the statute’s textual limitation; recognizing treble-damages RICO claims for lost earnings and medical costs flowing from personal injury would, as a practical matter, convert civil RICO into a broad personal-injury tort regime beyond what Congress authorized. Respect for text, history, and workability therefore counsels that derivative economic losses from personal injury are not cognizable “business or property” injuries under § 1964(c).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1964(c) authorizes suit only for a person “injured in his business or property,” and the ordinary public meaning of that phrase, modeled on Clayton Act § 4, excludes personal injuries and their derivative components. In Reiter v. Sonotone Corp., the Court recognized that “business or property” must exclude “personal injuries suffered,” and economic losses that are inseparable from a personal injury (lost earnings or medical expenses) are best understood as derivative of that excluded category rather than an independent injury to “business or property.” Sedima cautions against importing extra-textual antitrust standing barriers, but enforcing the statute’s own “business or property” limitation is textual, not extra-textual, and it preserves methodological consistency with Congress’s choice to withhold treble-damages recovery for personal-injury-type harms. Allowing recovery whenever a personal injury produces economic consequences would effectively erase the limiting words Congress used and expand civil RICO into a general treble-damages tort regime.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1964(c) authorizes suit only for a person “injured in his business or property,” and this Court has treated the identical Clayton Act language as “restrictive” and as excluding “personal injuries” and damages that are ultimately personal-injury recoveries. Reiter v. Sonotone Corp., 442 U.S. 330, 338–39 (1979), contrasted business/property harms with “damages resulting from a personal injury,” and its reasoning aligns with the concern that allowing lost earnings or medical expenses purely derivative of bodily harm would effectively convert civil RICO into a treble-damages personal-injury regime beyond what Congress specified in § 1964(c). Sedima, S.P.R.L. v. Imrex Co., 473 U.S. 479 (1985), teaches that civil RICO should be applied as written, but the written limitation here (“business or property”) forecloses claims where the only alleged economic loss flows from a personal injury. That construction also promotes administrable, procedurally fair boundaries on RICO standing and avoids massive, unintended expansion of federal racketeering litigation into routine tort disputes.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a plaintiff may sue under civil RICO for lost wages and other economic losses that flow from a personal injury, on the theory that those downstream monetary losses are injuries to the plaintiff’s “business or property.”
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1964(c) (civil RICO cause of action requiring injury to “business or property by reason of” a RICO violation).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that § 1964(c)’s “injured in his business or property” requirement excludes personal injuries and, critically, also excludes economic damages that are derivative of personal injuries (e.g., lost earnings, medical expenses, diminished earning capacity). They contend that allowing such claims would convert RICO into a treble-damages personal-injury/tort superstatute, contrary to the text, history, and the traditional line between personal-injury harms and property/business harms. They also emphasize administrability and limiting principles: if personal-injury-based wage loss counts as ‘business or property’ injury, civil RICO would invite expansive, punitive litigation well beyond the statute’s intended core and create massive spillover into product-liability and consumer-injury disputes.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues that even if RICO does not permit recovery for the personal injury itself (pain, suffering, bodily harm), the statute does permit recovery for concrete economic harms that are recognizable property interests—such as lost wages/earnings—because they represent money the plaintiff would have had but for the defendant’s racketeering conduct. In this view, the relevant injury is an economic/property injury (lost income), and it was caused ‘by reason of’ the RICO violation; excluding such losses would read ‘property’ too narrowly and undercut RICO’s remedial purpose where predicate acts (e.g., fraud) foreseeably cause economic consequences, even when the causal chain includes physical injury.
key_precedents: Sedima, S.P.R.L. v. Imrex Co., 473 U.S. 479 (1985)

John Roberts.reasoning: The strongest respondent point remains that lost wages and medical expenses are concrete economic harms and therefore “property,” but, as Justice Kagan stresses, reading § 1964(c) that way collapses the limiting work of the composite phrase “business or property” by allowing routine personal-injury damages to be repackaged as economic loss. Reiter’s construction of identical Clayton Act language—emphasized by Justice Gorsuch and Justice Alito—treats the phrase as having restrictive significance that excludes personal-injury damages and their inseparable derivatives, and we should not create a RICO-specific expansion absent clearer congressional direction. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Holmes reinforces that proximate-cause doctrine cannot substitute for the threshold category requirement; it may screen some attenuated claims, but it does not answer what injuries qualify in the first place. A narrow holding barring recovery for economic losses that are dependent on an underlying bodily injury best respects text, precedent, and administrability without opining broadly on other intangible property interests.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Respondent’s best point is that lost wages and medical bills are economic harms that sound like “property” in ordinary speech, but that reads the key phrase in isolation and ignores its historically understood limiting function. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, Reiter’s construction of the identical Clayton Act language gives “business or property” restrictive significance that excludes personal injuries and efforts to repackage their pecuniary sequelae; otherwise the line Congress adopted does no work. Justice Gorsuch’s copied-text point reinforces the originalist inference that Congress incorporated the settled meaning rather than creating a RICO-specific expansion into treble-damages personal-injury law. Sedima, as Justice Alito notes, rejected judge-made standing barriers, but it does not authorize us to dilute an express textual element—injury to “business or property”—as originally understood.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The strongest argument for Respondent would be that lost wages and medical bills are concrete economic harms and thus “property” in ordinary speech, but that reading ignores the limiting function of the phrase “injured in his business or property” as this Court has consistently treated it in the Clayton Act context. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas are right that Reiter’s description of the phrase’s “restrictive significance” would be largely nullified if plaintiffs could simply relabel the pecuniary consequences of bodily injury as a property injury and thereby trigger treble damages under § 1964(c). Sedima does not help Respondent because it rejected extra-textual standing barriers, not the statute’s express exclusion of personal-injury harms and their derivatives. Practical consequences reinforce the textual line: accepting derivative personal-injury losses would federalize large swaths of state tort law and turn RICO into a general tort multiplier without clear congressional authorization.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s best point is that lost wages and medical bills are concrete economic harms, and excluding them may feel in tension with RICO’s remedial aims for vulnerable plaintiffs. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief stress, Reiter’s reading of the identical Clayton Act phrase gives “business or property” restrictive significance; letting plaintiffs recover the economic consequences of bodily injury would effectively erase that textual boundary and transform civil RICO into a treble-damages personal-injury regime. Justice Jackson’s administrability and federalism concerns reinforce my pragmatic view: once derivative personal-injury losses count, the litigation universe expands dramatically and unpredictably, burdening courts and displacing state tort systems without clear congressional authorization. Sedima’s pro-remedial language doesn’t justify diluting an express statutory element, so I remain with petitioner on a narrow rule barring recovery for economic losses inseparable from personal injury.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best point is that lost wages and medical expenses look like classic “property” losses in ordinary speech, but Chief Justice Roberts is right that the operative phrase is the composite “business or property,” which our Clayton Act cases treat as a limiting term with “restrictive significance.” Reiter’s parallel construction of identical language matters here: it would be largely nullified if plaintiffs could recover whenever they can translate a personal injury into downstream pecuniary consequences. Justice Jackson’s Holmes-based proximate-cause point reinforces (but doesn’t replace) the threshold requirement: proximate cause screens who may sue, while “business or property” defines what kinds of injuries are cognizable, and these losses are inseparable from the underlying bodily harm. Sedima’s warning against extra-textual barriers doesn’t undermine this conclusion because we are applying an express statutory element as historically understood, not inventing a new standing hurdle.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that lost wages and medical expenses are “property” in ordinary parlance—fails because it atomizes the phrase “injured in his business or property” and drains it of the restrictive function Congress imported from Clayton Act § 4. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Reiter is decisive under a textualist methodology: when Congress borrows a settled phrase, we presume it carries its established limitation, and Reiter makes clear the limitation excludes personal-injury damages even when repackaged as economic loss. Justice Jackson’s Holmes-based administrability concerns confirm that proximate-cause screening cannot substitute for the statute’s threshold category of cognizable injury; letting derivative pecuniary harms qualify would collapse the line and effectively create a treble-damages personal-injury regime. Sedima does not undermine this conclusion because applying the “business or property” requirement enforces an express element rather than inventing an extra-textual standing barrier.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The strongest respondent contention—that lost wages and medical expenses are concrete economic harms and therefore “property”—still fails because it would collapse the limiting function of the borrowed term of art “injured in his business or property.” Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s reliance on Reiter is decisive for me: Reiter treated the identical Clayton Act phrase as having “restrictive significance” that excludes personal-injury damages, and that restriction is nullified if plaintiffs can repackage the pecuniary consequences of bodily harm as property loss. Justice Jackson’s Holmes/administrability point reinforces the practical problem that proximate-cause limits cannot substitute for the statute’s threshold injury category and would invite ordinary tort claims into treble-damages RICO. Sedima does not undermine this conclusion because we are not adding an extra-textual standing hurdle; we are enforcing an express textual element as historically understood.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Respondent’s best point remains that lost wages and medical expenses are tangible economic harms and thus “property” in ordinary parlance, bolstered by RICO’s remedial aims. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch stress, Congress borrowed the composite phrase “injured in his business or property” from the Clayton Act, and our Reiter line gives that phrase “restrictive significance” that excludes personal injuries and efforts to repackage their downstream pecuniary consequences as property harm. Accepting Respondent’s framing would effectively collapse the statutory boundary and convert § 1964(c) into a treble-damages personal-injury regime, a result the text—read in light of its established term-of-art meaning—does not support. Justice Jackson’s administrability/proximate-cause concerns in the Holmes tradition reinforce, rather than replace, that threshold textual limitation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that lost wages and medical bills are concrete economic harms that sound like “property” in ordinary language—has force, especially given RICO’s remedial aims, but it cannot overcome the limiting function of the composite phrase “injured in his business or property.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Reiter’s construction of the identical Clayton Act language treats that phrase as carrying “restrictive significance” that excludes personal-injury damages and their repackaging; accepting derivative pecuniary losses would effectively erase that boundary and convert § 1964(c) into a treble-damages personal-injury regime without clear textual authorization. Sedima does not push the other way because applying an express statutory element is not an extra-textual standing barrier, and (as I noted with Holmes) proximate-cause doctrine is not a workable substitute for defining what counts as a qualifying category of injury in the first instance. The pragmatic consequences—administrability, federalism, and the predictable spillover of ordinary tort claims into civil RICO—reinforce, but do not drive, the textual and precedent-based conclusion.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1964(c) limits civil RICO plaintiffs to those “injured in [their] business or property,” and this Court has long treated that identical language in the Clayton Act as carrying “restrictive significance” that excludes personal injuries. Reiter v. Sonotone Corp., 442 U.S. 330, 338–39 (1979), and related antitrust cases recognize that plaintiffs may not repackage “damages resulting from a personal injury” as business-or-property harm, and the same textual limitation naturally applies to RICO. Allowing lost wages and medical expenses that flow from bodily injury to qualify would substantially expand RICO into a treble-damages personal-injury regime, raising administrability and federalism concerns and risking institutional overreach absent clearer congressional instruction. A narrow holding that derivative economic losses from personal injury are not cognizable under § 1964(c) respects the statutory line and preserves doctrinal coherence with our parallel construction of comparable remedial schemes.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1964(c) authorizes suit only by a person “injured in his business or property,” text that—by its ordinary meaning and common-law backdrop—draws a sharp line between injuries to person and injuries to property. This Court has treated the identical “business or property” language in the Clayton Act as having “restrictive significance” that excludes personal injuries, Reiter v. Sonotone Corp., 442 U.S. 330, 339 (1979), and that exclusion necessarily prevents plaintiffs from recasting personal-injury harms as “business or property” claims by pleading derivative economic losses like lost wages or medical expenses. Allowing such downstream losses would collapse the textual limitation and effectively convert RICO into a treble-damages personal-injury regime, contrary to § 1964(c)’s terms and this Court’s repeated parallel construction of Clayton Act and RICO language (including Sedima’s insistence on adhering to the statute’s elements). The proper reading therefore bars civil RICO recovery where the asserted “property” loss merely flows from a personal injury rather than an independent injury to business or property.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1964(c) limits civil RICO to plaintiffs “injured in [their] business or property,” and that restrictive phrase—borrowed from Clayton Act § 4—has long been understood to exclude personal injuries and attempts to repackage personal-injury harms as economic loss. In Reiter v. Sonotone Corp., 442 U.S. 330, 339 (1979), this Court emphasized the phrase’s “restrictive significance” and its function in excluding personal-injury damages, a reading that naturally applies to RICO’s identical language. Allowing lost wages or medical expenses that are derivative of a personal injury would erase that boundary and effectively convert RICO’s treble-damages remedy into a general tort multiplier, a result inconsistent with the statute’s text and administrable limiting principles. Sedima does not authorize courts to expand the “business or property” element; it rejected extra-textual standing barriers, not the statute’s express limitation in § 1964(c).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1964(c) authorizes suit only for injury to “business or property,” and this Court has read identical language in the Clayton Act as carrying “restrictive significance” that “exclude[s] personal injuries.” Reiter v. Sonotone Corp., 442 U.S. 330, 339 (1979). That exclusion would be largely nullified if plaintiffs could repackage personal-injury harms as downstream economic losses like lost wages or medical expenses, effectively converting civil RICO into a treble-damages personal-injury regime beyond Congress’s chosen text. Whatever RICO’s remedial aims (Sedima, S.P.R.L. v. Imrex Co., 473 U.S. 479 (1985)), they cannot override the statutory limitation that the injury itself be to “business or property,” which here is derivative of bodily harm rather than an independent property injury.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1964(c) authorizes suit only for injury to “business or property,” and this Court has long treated that phrase—borrowed verbatim from the Clayton Act—as having “restrictive significance” that “exclude[s] personal injuries.” Reiter v. Sonotone Corp., 442 U.S. 330, 339 (1979). Allowing recovery for lost wages and medical expenses when those losses are derivative of a personal injury would effectively erase that limiting line and risk transforming civil RICO into a treble-damages personal-injury regime, a result difficult to square with the text’s exclusion and with administrable boundaries. Consistent with Reiter and our practice of reading identical language in parallel (see also Sedima, 473 U.S. 479 (1985), rejecting extra-textual limits but not rewriting “business or property”), downstream pecuniary consequences of bodily harm are not themselves injuries to “business or property” within § 1964(c).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1964(c) authorizes suit only for a person “injured in his business or property by reason of” a RICO violation, and the ordinary meaning of that limitation, reflected in the identical Clayton Act phrase, excludes personal injuries and efforts to repackage them as downstream economic losses. In Reiter v. Sonotone Corp., the Court treated “business or property” as a restrictive category that excludes “damages for personal injuries,” and that understanding has long informed parallel interpretation of RICO’s copied text. Allowing lost wages and similar pecuniary consequences that flow from bodily harm would erase the statute’s textual boundary and effectively convert RICO into a treble-damages personal-injury regime—an expansion Congress did not enact. Sedima cautions against importing antitrust-specific standing barriers into RICO, but it does not authorize courts to ignore § 1964(c)’s threshold requirement that the injury be to “business or property,” not personal injury and its derivatives.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1964(c) limits civil RICO suits to plaintiffs “injured in [their] business or property,” and that restrictive phrase, borrowed from the Clayton Act, has long been understood to exclude personal injuries and efforts to repackage personal-injury harms as “property” losses. Reiter v. Sonotone Corp. confirms that “business or property” does not encompass “personal injuries suffered,” and allowing lost wages or medical expenses that are derivative of bodily injury would largely erase that line and convert RICO into a treble-damages personal-injury superstatute. Sedima cautions against importing antitrust-specific standing barriers, but it does not authorize courts to expand the statute’s text beyond its historical meaning; here, the history and tradition of the phrase point the other way. Practical workability also favors Petitioners: a derivative-loss rule provides a clearer, more administrable boundary and avoids sweeping RICO into routine tort and products-liability disputes.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1964(c) authorizes suit only for injury to “business or property,” language that in its ordinary meaning draws a line between proprietary/commercial harms and personal injuries. This Court has treated the identical “business or property” limitation in the Clayton Act as “restrictive” and as excluding “personal injuries,” Reiter v. Sonotone Corp., 442 U.S. 330, 339 (1979), and that exclusion would be evaded if plaintiffs could repackage the economic consequences of a personal injury (lost wages, medical expenses) as stand-alone property injuries. Sedima confirms that civil RICO’s private right of action is bounded by the statutory elements, and expanding “business or property” to encompass derivative personal-injury losses would transform RICO into a treble-damages personal-injury statute without textual warrant. Respect for administrable limits and methodological consistency with this Court’s parallel interpretation of “business or property” counsel against allowing recovery for downstream economic losses that are inseparable from an underlying personal injury.

Reiter v. Sonotone Corp., 442 U.S. 330, 339 (1979). Allowing recovery for lost wages and medical expenses that are derivative of bodily harm would effectively collapse that limiting line and transform civil RICO into a treble-damages personal-injury regime, a practical consequence inconsistent with the statute’s text and structure. Moreover, RICO’s “by reason of” requirement incorporates proximate-cause constraints, Holmes v. SIPC, 503 U.S. 258, 267 (1992), and derivative personal-injury economic losses raise administrability and causation complications that counsel a narrower reading.
